# The Office of Lost Time

The Office of Lost Time occupied the second floor of a building that had once sold pianos. On damp mornings, the staircase smelled faintly of felt and varnish. A brass plate beside the entrance listed the opening hours as NINE UNTIL SUFFICIENT, which newcomers generally took to be a joke.

It was not a joke, although the staff disagreed about what it meant.

Mara had worked there for eleven years. Her job was to receive claims, establish eligibility, and explain that certain kinds of time could not be returned.

“No,” she said to a man in a cycling helmet, “we cannot reimburse a marriage.”

“Not even part of one?”

“Not as a single claim.”

He considered this.

“What if I itemize?”

She slid the appropriate form across the counter.

There were rules. Time spent waiting for a late train could be recovered. Time spent looking for glasses already on your head could not, because the department classified that as an educational expense. Time lost to administrative error was fully refundable, provided the error had been made by another office.

Their own errors were handled upstairs.

There was no upstairs.

Mara did not make the rules. She knew this because she had once submitted a proposal to change one and had received a letter thanking her for her interest in local government.

At eleven each morning, her colleague Ivo brought tea in two unmatched cups.

“Anything interesting?”

“A marriage.”

“Again?”

“He may itemize.”

Ivo nodded. “Ambitious.”

***

Returned time arrived in small glass cylinders, sealed with gray wax. A cylinder containing seven minutes was no larger than a sewing needle. An hour could fit comfortably in a coat pocket. Anything beyond a day required collection by an accredited carrier.

The cylinders did not glow. People were often disappointed by this.

To use one, you broke the seal.

The world then continued without you for the specified interval, while you remained in a private allotment of ordinary time. You could sleep, read, peel potatoes, or sit on the edge of your bed and fail to decide what to do.

You could not travel backward. You could not bring anyone with you. Nothing you did could affect another living person until the interval ended.

These conditions appeared in bold print on every receipt.

Nevertheless, people asked.

“Could I see my mother?”

“Not through our office.”

“Could I finish a conversation?”

“Only your side.”

“Could I be young?”

“You would be exactly as old as you are.”

This last answer caused the most trouble.

People imagined that time, once recovered, would arrive with its original weather and the strength they had possessed when they lost it. Instead, a retired mason received the forty-three minutes he had spent outside a locked supply depot in 1968 and used them to take a bath.

He later wrote to say it had been an excellent bath.

Mara kept his letter in her desk. She had shown it to Ivo so often that he could recite it.

***

One Thursday in November, a woman brought in a cardboard box held together with blue string.

She was perhaps seventy, with the upright posture of someone who had spent years carrying things without assistance.

“My husband died in September,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“Yes,” the woman said, acknowledging this as one might acknowledge rain. “He left these.”

Inside the box were cylinders. Hundreds of them. Some were thin as fish bones; others had the solid dimensions of fountain pens. All remained sealed.

Mara lifted one carefully.

“Your husband made these claims?”

“Over forty years.”

“Did he ever use any?”

“Not that I know of.”

Mara checked the registry. The husband’s name was Emil Voss. There were six hundred and twelve approved claims under his account.

Delayed buses. Canceled appointments. A mistaken hospital admission. Eleven hours in a lift. Three days lost when a ferry company sent him to the wrong island.

“He was saving them,” the woman said.

“For what?”

“For when things settled down.”

The office grew quiet around them. Outside, someone was reversing a delivery van, its warning bell sounding at patient intervals.

“I’d like them transferred to me.”

Mara turned the cylinder between her fingers.

“Recovered time is nontransferable.”

The woman looked at the box.

“Well,” she said. “Of course it is.”

It was not an angry remark. Mara would have preferred an angry remark.

She gave the woman a claim review form, although she knew exactly how the review would end.

***

At lunch, Mara ate a pear over the wastebasket.

“Six hundred and twelve,” she told Ivo.

“How much altogether?”

“About nine weeks.”

Ivo stopped stirring his soup.

“Good grief.”

“He saved nine weeks and then died.”

“People save all sorts of things.”

“Not usually nine weeks.”

“My aunt had a cupboard full of wrapping paper. We buried her on a Tuesday. On Wednesday I used some of it for a wedding present.”

Mara looked at him.

“I’m not comparing them,” he said. “I’m saying the cupboard was full.”

After lunch, she went into the records room.

The oldest claims were written in brown ink on cards with softened corners. Before cylinders, the office had issued folded paper packets. Before packets, there had apparently been a system involving knots, although nobody still employed understood the filing method.

Mara searched for precedents.

She found a sailor whose unused time had been returned to the sea. A teacher had requested that hers be divided among her pupils, but the application had been rejected because several were already adults. One man had asked to be buried with his accumulated hours.

Permission granted, the record said.

Then, beneath that, in another hand:

Not recommended. Groundskeeper reported persistent knocking.

At four, Mara found a regulation headed DISPOSAL OF UNREDEEMED PERSONAL CHRONOLOGIES.

The relevant paragraph was short.

In the absence of an eligible beneficiary, recovered intervals may be released into the municipal commons.

There was no definition of municipal commons.

There was, however, a form.

***

Her supervisor, Mr. Pell, wore knitted waistcoats and distrusted questions that began with “technically.”

“Technically,” Mara said, “we can release Mr. Voss’s time into the municipal commons.”

“No.”

“You haven’t heard the proposal.”

“I’ve heard the first word.”

She put the regulation on his desk.

He read it twice.

“This refers to an obsolete practice.”

“It’s still a current regulation.”

“So is the requirement that we maintain a hitching post.”

“We do maintain a hitching post.”

“That is a bicycle rack.”

“It was reclassified in 1987.”

Mr. Pell removed his spectacles.

“What do you imagine would happen?”

“I don’t know.”

“That is not a strong opening.”

“We could find out.”

He looked through the glass partition toward the waiting room. Four people sat beneath a poster reminding them that impatience did not constitute additional loss.

“Public time is complicated,” he said.

“Private time seems complicated too.”

“Private time is administered by the individual. When they misuse it, they can hardly write to the council.”

“They do.”

“Yes, but the council forwards it to us.”

He handed back the regulation.

“Get written consent from the widow. Get a location. Get a statement of risks.”

“What risks?”

“That,” said Mr. Pell, “is what the statement must establish.”

As Mara reached the door, he added, “No public announcements.”

She turned.

“We are not advertising free time,” he said. “Can you imagine the queue?”

From the waiting room came the sharp sound of someone tearing up a form.

Mr. Pell shut his eyes.

***

Mrs. Voss lived above a bakery on a street where the trees had lifted the pavement into ridges.

She served coffee in cups so small that Mara worried she might swallow hers accidentally.

“Release it where?” Mrs. Voss asked.

“A public place. A square, perhaps. A park.”

“And then?”

“We’re not certain.”

“Would people get younger?”

“No.”

“Would they notice?”

“Possibly.”

Mrs. Voss looked toward the window.

Below them, a baker in a floury apron was smoking beside a stack of delivery crates. He held the cigarette away from his body, as though hoping to establish that it belonged to someone else.

“Emil hated waste,” she said. “He cut the mold off cheese until there was hardly any cheese left. He kept screws in jam jars. Every time we bought a new kettle, he saved the old flex.”

“Was he happy?”

The question escaped before Mara could make it more professional.

Mrs. Voss considered.

“Frequently. But he rarely admitted it until afterward.”

She stood and took a photograph from the mantelpiece. A younger Emil was sitting in a deck chair, holding a peach. His expression suggested that the photographer had interrupted something important.

“That was the wrong island,” she said.

“The ferry claim?”

“We had a lovely time.”

Mara studied the photograph.

“He claimed three days.”

“He had principles.”

Mrs. Voss returned the frame to its place.

“There’s a little square behind the old market. Emil used to eat his lunch there. Would that do?”

“I think so.”

“Then do that.”

***

The square behind the old market contained four benches, a dry fountain, and a tree whose roots had broken the fountain’s supply pipe twenty years earlier.

The council had decided that repairing the pipe might damage the tree. Removing the tree might damage the fountain. Leaving both alone had eventually become policy.

Mara visited on Friday afternoon.

A courier ate noodles from a paper carton. Two schoolgirls shared earphones. A man in a dark overcoat sat with a shopping bag between his shoes, doing nothing Mara could identify.

She tried to imagine nine weeks entering the square.

Would every person receive nine weeks? Would the time divide itself among them? Would the pigeons qualify? What about the tree, which was already very good at occupying time without appearing to spend it?

She wrote these questions in her notebook.

Under STATEMENT OF RISKS, she wrote:

Uncertain distribution.

Then:

Potential effects on wildlife.

Then, after some thought:

Possibility of disappointment.

On Monday, Mr. Pell read the statement.

“You cannot list disappointment as a risk.”

“It seems like the main one.”

“If we listed disappointment as a risk, we would never do anything.”

Mara waited.

He sighed and signed.

They scheduled the release for Wednesday at twelve seventeen. This was not a significant time. It was simply when Ivo could cover the counter.

Mrs. Voss said she would come.

“Should I bring anything?”

“No.”

“I’ll bring sandwiches.”

Mara nearly said they would not be necessary, but found herself asking for cheese.

***

The cylinders made a surprisingly heavy burden.

Mara carried them in the original box, with the blue string replaced. Mrs. Voss brought sandwiches wrapped in greaseproof paper.

They sat beside the fountain.

“How do we do it?” Mrs. Voss asked.

Mara unfolded the instructions she had found attached to the old regulation.

“We open them.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“This could take a while.”

It did.

The wax was brittle on the older cylinders, stubborn on the newer ones. Mara used a small knife. Mrs. Voss employed a hairpin with impressive efficiency.

Nothing happened.

They opened delayed trains, missed connections, a printer’s error that had cost Emil an afternoon. They opened the lift and the hospital and the wrong island.

A breeze moved through the square.

The courier arrived with his noodles. The schoolgirls passed along the far side of the fountain. Somewhere behind the market, bottles crashed into a recycling bin.

Mara broke the final seal.

Mrs. Voss looked around.

“Is that it?”

“I don’t know.”

They waited.

The man with the shopping bag came and sat on the opposite bench.

A pigeon approached Mrs. Voss with the brisk entitlement of a minor official.

“Well,” she said, opening the sandwiches, “we might as well.”

Mara took one.

It was cheese, with pickle cut into small uneven pieces.

She had not realized how hungry she was.

For a little while, neither woman spoke.

Then Mrs. Voss said, “He always ate the crusts first. Emil. Did you know anyone else who did that?”

***

Mara returned to the office at one eleven.

Ivo looked up.

“You’re early.”

“I’m late.”

“It’s twelve nineteen.”

The wall clock agreed with him.

Mara checked her watch. Twelve nineteen.

She looked back toward the stairs.

“What happened?” Ivo asked.

“I’m not sure.”

That afternoon, three people missed appointments because they believed the clocks had stopped. A market porter completed an entire crossword during his smoking break. The courier reported that his noodles had remained hot for what seemed an unreasonable length of time.

The schoolgirls returned to the square after lessons and sat until dark.

No official complaints were filed.

Over the following weeks, the effects became harder to document.

People who sat in the square sometimes found that they had enough time to finish things. Not large things. A letter. An argument. An orange.

A woman who worked at the pharmacy went there between shifts and discovered she could remember a dream from beginning to end.

The fountain remained dry.

The tree lost its leaves.

Nobody grew younger. Nobody met the dead. The pigeons, so far as anyone could tell, experienced no administrative difficulties.

Mr. Pell requested a report.

Mara wrote six pages, then reduced them to one.

“How long will it last?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Can we repeat it?”

“Possibly.”

“Can we measure it?”

“Not yet.”

He read her conclusion.

“You’ve written, ‘People seem less hurried.’”

“Yes.”

“That is not a unit.”

“No,” Mara said. “It isn’t.”

He left the sentence in.

***

In December, Mara found a cylinder in the back of her own desk.

Seventeen minutes. A canceled dental appointment, years earlier.

She had forgotten it completely.

At lunchtime, she took it to the square.

Mrs. Voss was there, feeding crumbs to a pigeon.

“You shouldn’t,” Mara said.

“I know.”

Mara showed her the cylinder.

“Another contribution?”

“Perhaps.”

But Mrs. Voss shook her head.

“You keep that one.”

“What for?”

“How should I know?”

Mara laughed and put it in her pocket.

They sat together beneath the bare tree. A delivery van rattled past the mouth of the square. Somewhere a radio was playing a song neither of them could quite identify.

After a while, Mrs. Voss began describing a shelf she wanted put up in her kitchen.

“Emil left plenty of screws,” she said.

“I can help on Saturday.”

“Morning?”

“Yes.”

The pharmacy woman arrived and sat down with her eyes closed.

Mara checked her watch, then tucked her hand back into her pocket around the cylinder. She would have to leave soon. There was time to hear about the shelf.
